extracted.intended_audience: military officers, government attorneys, claimants, and officials handling claims or command authority issues involving the United States
extracted.subtask_description: Compilation of legal rules and standards governing (1) when the United States (or its departments) may be held liable or may pay claims, and (2) rules on eligibility, delegation, and limits of military command and related authorities. Intended as reference for adjudicating claims and for military/government officials on command powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Testimony exemption for public-business matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Government employees summoned as witnesses in private litigation are not required to testify regarding matters of public business if, in the opinion of the head of a department, the disclosure would injuriously affect the public interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies where department head judges disclosure harmful to public interest; exempts employees from testifying in private litigation on public business matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rebellion-disqualification is personal only (section 3480)
rubrics_metrics.description: The provision making it unlawful to pay certain claims against the United States to persons who promoted the late rebellion creates a personal disability only and does not operate against the heirs of those disqualified unless the heirs also participated in the rebellion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disqualification for payment is personal to the participant in rebellion; heirs remain eligible unless they themselves participated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liability depends on official capacity/benefit (relief agent doctrine)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a private vessel is used in connection with relief work and officers gave orders as relief agents (not as representatives of the United States), the use does not benefit the Army or Navy and the United States is not liable to compensate the owners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Liability to the United States for use of private property hinges on whether the use was for and benefited the military/government or was merely relief activity by officers acting in a non-governmental capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: U.S. not liable for private counsel in court-martial defense
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim by an attorney for services rendered as counsel for an accused officer in a court-martial trial is without merit as against the United States; the Government has nothing to do with its payment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defense counsel fees in court-martial matters are not payable by the United States absent specific statutory authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: No statutory provision for certain travel/collection expenses
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims for time, cost, and expenses incurred in going to collect fees due a civilian witness before a court-martial have no statutory basis for payment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absent a law specifically authorizing payment, such claims should be denied.

rubrics_metrics.name: No claim for detention awaiting trial absent statute
rubrics_metrics.description: A soldier (or civilian wrongly detained on suspicion of desertion) has no legal claim for damages against the United States for a period during which he was detained awaiting trial or clearance, even if innocent in fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relief for detention-related damages requires express statutory authorization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticated departmental copies admissible (sec. 882 R.S.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Copies of books, records, papers, or documents in any executive department, authenticated under departmental seals, shall be admitted in evidence equally with the originals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Departments should follow their rules on attestation; attested transcripts of public records are not to be entrusted to private persons for controversies in which the United States has no real interest except on tribunal certificate that transcripts are essential to ends of justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive departments cannot pay damages for construction employment absent statute
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no law authorizing executive departments to pay claims for damages on account of injuries received by persons employed in construction of public buildings or river and harbor improvements; absent statute the department is without power to pay them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims of this type require a legislative appropriation or other statutory authority before payment can be made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deficiency deduction statute applies only to actual officers (sec. 1304 R.S.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section requiring that a deficiency charged against an officer be deducted from his monthly pay (unless he shows the deficiency wasn't occasioned by his fault) applies only to actual officers of the Army and cannot be extended to a claim by a person formerly in the Army but long a civilian.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deficiency rules are limited to persons currently holding the specified official status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Erroneous payment recovery: bank vs United States
rubrics_metrics.description: When a pay certificate erroneously given to a soldier was indorsed and presented by banks and paid by a paymaster, the second bank that refunded the paymaster has no legal claim against the United States; its recourse is against the first bank.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an erroneous payment is discovered, the remedy of intermediaries is a private action, not a claim against the United States.

rubrics_metrics.name: Loss of private property on U.S. ships requires Congress for payment
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims by contract personnel (e.g., contract nurse) for loss of private property by sinking of a United States hospital ship cannot be paid without special authority from Congress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compensation for private property losses involving government vessels demands explicit Congressional appropriation or authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: U.S. not insurer for personal baggage during government-paid transport
rubrics_metrics.description: When an officer's personal baggage transported at government expense is broken into and property stolen, remedy is against the railroad company and not against the United States; the United States does not make itself an insurer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims should generally be pursued against the carrier, not the United States, unless the loss is directly attributable to government negligence creating liability.

rubrics_metrics.name: No War Department appropriation for registered mail lost on Army transport
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no appropriation under the War Department from which the sender of a registered mail package lost while on board an Army transport can be paid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absent an appropriation, claims for lost registered mail on Army transports must be denied or referred to Congress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lease-related incidental expenses not payable separately
rubrics_metrics.description: Where lands were leased for maneuvers and a lessor claimed cost of forage necessary to feed stock kept off pastures during maneuvers, such expense was a necessary incident to the operation of the lease and the claim was denied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expenses that are normal incidents of the lease relationship are not compensable separately as claims against the Government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heads of departments cannot employ private counsel at Government expense (secs. 1876, 365 R.S.)
rubrics_metrics.description: No head of a department shall employ an attorney or counsel at the expense of the United States; when in need of counsel they shall call upon the Department of Justice. Consequently, departmental secretaries have no authority to pay private attorneys for services to the Government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims for private legal services rendered on behalf of the Government are generally barred; payment requires statutory authorization or referral to DOJ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Payment for attorney services in certain prisoner/habeas matters prohibited absent special act
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an attorney submitted a claim for services rendered an enlisted man in a habeas corpus proceeding without prior notice of employment, the employment and payment were prohibited by sections 189 and 365 R.S., and payment could not be made except by special act of Congress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal representation expenses for enlisted personnel in such contexts are not payable absent explicit Congressional appropriation.

rubrics_metrics.name: U.S. not liable for coroner fees in inquests over deceased soldiers
rubrics_metrics.description: The United States is not liable for fees and expenses of a coroner in holding an inquest over a deceased soldier; no officer is authorized to bind the Government for such services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coroner expenses in these circumstances are not chargeable to the United States absent special authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive cannot appropriate money on own authority to satisfy claims
rubrics_metrics.description: An executive official cannot, of his own authority, appropriate the money of the United States for the purpose of satisfying a claim; reimbursement for taxes assessed by military authorities expended in public service required Congressional action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All appropriations to satisfy claims or reimbursements must be made by Congress, not by unilateral executive action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paymaster recourse after being 'held responsible' (Court of Claims under sec. 1059 R.S.)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a paymaster seeks relief from liability for public funds stolen while in his charge, he should credit himself in his accounts; if disallowed at the Treasury, his recourse is an application for relief to the Court of Claims under section 1059 R.S. The right to recourse accrues only after the disbursing officer has been 'held responsible' by the accounting officers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrative accounting determinations must first be made; judicial recourse follows only after being formally held responsible by accounting officers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government not liable for property stolen from government storehouse
rubrics_metrics.description: Where personal property of an officer is stored in a Government storehouse during absence and is stolen, the Government is not liable for the loss.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Storage in government facilities does not automatically create government liability for theft; specific statutory or contractual obligations would be required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purchaser's title limited to vendor's title — claimant entitled if proves ownership
rubrics_metrics.description: If a private person later claims a horse purchased by the Government alleging it was stolen, the claimant, if he can establish ownership, is entitled to it because a vendor can grant no better title than he had; the Government should notify vendor to defend any replevin action and preserve rights to sue for warranty of title.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When claimants prove title superior to vendor, the claimant's right is recognized; Government may pursue vendor subsequently for breach of warranty.

rubrics_metrics.name: No authority for extra compensation to officer acting as court-martial clerk
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim by an officer to be allowed extra compensation for services rendered as clerk to a general court-martial of which he was the junior member was without sanction in law or regulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extra compensation claims require statutory or regulatory sanction; ad hoc payments are not authorized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between 'rank' and 'command' — rank alone doesn't convey command
rubrics_metrics.description: The terms 'rank' and 'command' are neither convertible nor synonymous; rank conveys eligibility to exercise command in the military service but does not itself authorize exercise of command — command must be conferred by statute or by assignment of the President.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Possession of military rank does not by itself authorize exercise of command; look for specific statutory grant or presidential assignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Staff officers generally limited to departmental control (no line command absent assignment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Staff officers exercise command or control in their own departments only and are expressly forbidden by law to exercise command in the line; however, by express order of the President and specific assignment they may exercise functions of any command in the line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Staff officers' authority is departmental unless specially assigned by the President.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detail to General Staff suspends line-command eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Under recent legislation officers of the line detailed for limited tenure to staff departments or the General Staff have their power to assume or exercise command in the line in abeyance during such incumbency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An officer detailed to staff positions temporarily forgoes the normal right to assume line command.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marine officers require presidential assignment to assume command in certain contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: A Marine officer returning from service could not legally assume command of troops on board a transport without a direct assignment by the President.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assignment of Marines to command positions in mixed-service contexts is constrained and often requires Presidential assignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil offices with attached rank do not automatically authorize command
rubrics_metrics.description: An office (e.g., assistant chief of Philippine Constabulary) that is civil in nature may have military rank attached by operation of law, but the attribution of rank conveys no right to exercise military command unless a special assignment by the President or appropriate statutory provision authorizes it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check the enabling statute (e.g., act of Jan 30, 1903) for the measure and scope of any command that may be exercised by holders of civil offices with rank.

rubrics_metrics.name: Command can only be delegated to seniors over juniors consistent with congressional rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Power to command can only be delegated to a senior to be exercised over juniors in rank; command must be exercised in accordance with legislation by Congress regarding rank and subordination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delegation of command must respect statutory grades and the system of military subordination established by Congress.

rubrics_metrics.name: President's authority to assume or delegate command
rubrics_metrics.description: The President, as Commander in Chief, may assume direct command of troops when necessary for the public interest, but in most cases must delegate command because he cannot be personally present everywhere; Congress has provided a class of officers to exercise delegated commands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presidential assumption or delegation of command is constitutional; look to specific orders or statutory delegations for validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: President authorized to detail officers for special purposes (e.g., engineers to Interior)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the detail of officers (e.g., Engineer Corps) is desired for questions committed to another department, the President is authorized under relevant statutes (e.g., sec. 1158 R.S.) to make such details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presidential detailing of officers to other departments for specialized tasks is permissible under statute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division/department commanders limited in assigning Marines and issuing certain orders
rubrics_metrics.description: A department or division commander is without authority to assign an officer or enlisted man of the Marine Corps to duty on shore or on an Army transport (such assignments can only be made by the President). Division commanders may not legally issue orders to sanitary inspectors directing inspections involving travel and claims for mileage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Certain cross-corps assignments and travel orders that implicate mileage/claims are beyond division/department commander authority and implicate higher authorization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post commanders' authority to reassign officers and control privileges
rubrics_metrics.description: A post commander may relieve an officer from duty with an organization and assign him to another; may withdraw the privilege of leaving post; may order an officer on detached service for observation purposes though generally cannot order travel involving payment of mileage unaided by superior authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Post commanders have broad administrative authority over personnel and privileges but financial obligations (mileage) may exceed their unilateral authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspension from pay and duty does not necessarily imply confinement
rubrics_metrics.description: A sentence of suspension from duty and pay for 15 days does not imply confinement to quarters or arrest; it is customary to allow an officer under such sentence the limits of his command.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish suspension from confinement; conditions of suspension are governed by custom and relevant orders/regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commander may regulate leave and marital privileges but cannot criminalize marriage
rubrics_metrics.description: A commander may refuse permission to leave to marry and may exclude soldiers' wives from a post if discipline requires, but he has no statutory authority to prohibit soldiers from contracting marriage or to make marriage itself a military offense; only Congress could legislatively restrict marriage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commanders control privileges affecting marriage but cannot criminalize the act of marrying without statutory backing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Soldier on bail may be required to perform duty with unaffected pay status
rubrics_metrics.description: A soldier arrested by civil authorities and released on bail may, on returning to station, be required to perform usual military duty appropriate to his rank, and while on duty his pay status remains unaffected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Civil arrest and bail do not automatically suspend military duty or alter pay status unless otherwise ordered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordering medically excused soldiers to duty entails command responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Although a post commander may order to duty a soldier excused by the surgeon for sickness or disability, if he does so he assumes responsibility for any material injury that may result and may be amenable to trial for the offense involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commanders should not order medically excused personnel to duty without recognizing potential liability for resulting harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Return of property improperly turned over following acquittal
rubrics_metrics.description: When a soldier is acquitted and property taken at arrest was improperly turned over to a private (e.g., post trader), the post commander should refund the amount to the soldier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Post commanders must take steps to restore property or value to the innocent soldier when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restitution to victim when proceeds of false pretenses found on accused
rubrics_metrics.description: When a convicted soldier obtained money from another by false pretenses and the unexpended balance is found on his person at arrest, the sum taken should be returned to the victim from whom it was obtained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts/command should ensure restitution to victims when identifiable proceeds remain recoverable from the offender.
